passage: Since the city installed brighter streetlights in the Eastside district last year, reported burglaries there have fallen by 20 percent. The city should therefore install brighter lights in every district to reduce burglary.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Reported burglaries fell by about 20 percent in every district last year, including those where the lights were not changed.
Brighter streetlights cost more to run than the old lights.
Some Eastside residents complained that the new lights were too bright.
Burglaries in the Eastside district usually happen at night.
The Eastside district has more shops than most other districts.
explanation: If burglaries fell just as much everywhere, the lights probably were not the cause. That attacks the causal link the argument depends on.

passage: Students who take the optional review course score higher on the final exam than students who do not. Therefore, the review course improves exam performance.
stem: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
choices: The students who take the course were not already stronger students before taking it.
The review course is taught by the same teacher as the main course.
Most students take the review course.
The final exam covers material from the review course.
Students enjoy the review course.
explanation: If stronger students choose the course, the higher scores could reflect who enrolls rather than what the course does. The argument must assume this is not the case.

passage: A study found that people who drink green tea daily have lower rates of heart disease. The researchers concluded that green tea protects the heart.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?
choices: The lower rates remained after the researchers accounted for diet, exercise and smoking.
Green tea is popular in many countries.
Some people who drink green tea also drink coffee.
Heart disease is a leading cause of death worldwide.
Green tea contains less caffeine than coffee.
explanation: Ruling out other lifestyle differences makes it more likely that tea itself, rather than habits that go with it, explains the difference.

passage: Every successful novelist I know writes every morning. So if you want to become a successful novelist, you should write every morning.
stem: The reasoning is most vulnerable to which criticism?
choices: It ignores the possibility that many unsuccessful writers also write every morning.
It assumes that all novelists are successful.
It relies on the opinion of a single novelist.
It confuses writing in the morning with writing at night.
It fails to define what a novel is.
explanation: Knowing that successful novelists write daily says nothing about whether daily writing leads to success, especially if many who write daily never succeed.

passage: The company's new hiring test predicts job performance well: employees hired since the test was introduced have received better reviews than those hired before.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choices: The company changed its review system at the same time, making reviews more generous for everyone.
The test takes an hour to complete.
Some applicants found the test difficult.
The company hired more people last year than the year before.
Several competitors use similar tests.
explanation: If reviews became more generous for everyone, newer employees' better reviews may reflect the new system, not the test.

passage: All the paintings in the exhibition were made before 1900. Some of the paintings in the exhibition are by artists who also made sculptures.
stem: If the statements are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: Some paintings made before 1900 are by artists who also made sculptures.
All artists who made sculptures painted before 1900.
No paintings made after 1900 are by sculptors.
Most paintings in the exhibition are by sculptors.
Some sculptures in the exhibition were made before 1900.
explanation: The paintings by sculptor-artists are in the exhibition, and every painting there was made before 1900, so some pre-1900 paintings are by such artists. The others go beyond what is given.

passage: To reduce traffic, the town plans to build a new road around the center. Drivers passing through will use the new road, so traffic in the center will fall.
stem: The plan's success depends on which assumption?
choices: A significant share of center traffic consists of drivers passing through rather than going to the center.
The new road will be finished on schedule.
Most residents support the plan.
The new road will be wider than the roads in the center.
Public transport in the town is poor.
explanation: A bypass only helps if many drivers in the center are just passing through. If most are going there, they will still come.

passage: After the library extended its opening hours, the number of books borrowed rose by 15 percent. The library director argues that the longer hours caused the increase.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most supports the director's argument?
choices: Most of the additional borrowing took place during the newly added hours.
The library added new books to its collection last year.
Nearby libraries have also extended their hours.
The library's staff numbers did not change.
Borrowing has risen slowly for several years.
explanation: If the extra borrowing happened in the new hours, the link between longer hours and more borrowing is direct. New books or a long-term trend would offer other explanations.

passage: Sales of electric bicycles rose sharply after the government offered a purchase subsidy. Officials conclude that the subsidy caused the rise.
stem: Which of the following, if true, casts the most doubt on the officials' conclusion?
choices: Sales had begun rising sharply six months before the subsidy was announced, after a large drop in battery prices.
The subsidy covered only part of the purchase price.
Electric bicycles are popular with commuters.
Some buyers did not know about the subsidy.
The government also subsidizes electric cars.
explanation: If the sharp rise started before the subsidy, driven by cheaper batteries, the subsidy is unlikely to be the main cause.

passage: A school replaced its printed textbooks with tablets. Test scores rose the following year. The principal claims that the tablets improved learning.
stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the principal's claim?
choices: Whether the school made other changes, such as new teachers or curriculum, in the same year
Whether the tablets were expensive
How many students own tablets at home
Whether students prefer tablets to books
What brand of tablet the school chose
explanation: Other changes made at the same time could explain the rise. Knowing whether there were any is key to judging the causal claim.

passage: No study has proven that the new food additive is harmful. Therefore, the additive is safe.
stem: The argument is flawed because it
choices: treats a lack of evidence of harm as proof of safety
relies on studies that were too small
assumes that all additives are harmful
confuses one additive with another
ignores the cost of the additive
explanation: Absence of proof of harm is not proof of safety: the additive may simply not have been studied well.

passage: Over the past decade, the number of doctors in the region has increased, yet patients report waiting longer for appointments than they did ten years ago.
stem: Which of the following, if true, best explains this apparent contradiction?
choices: The region's population has grown much faster than its number of doctors.
Many doctors in the region trained abroad.
Doctors' salaries have risen over the decade.
Some patients prefer to see the same doctor every time.
Appointment booking moved online during the decade.
explanation: If demand grew faster than supply, there are fewer doctors per patient despite more doctors overall, so waits get longer.

passage: The museum should charge for entry. Visitors who pay will value the collection more, and so will be more careful not to damage it.
stem: The argument assumes that
choices: valuing a collection more makes visitors more careful with it
most damage to the collection is caused by visitors
free museums attract more visitors
the museum needs more money
visitors would rather pay than not
explanation: The conclusion follows only if valuing the collection more actually changes how carefully people behave.

passage: People who live near parks report higher life satisfaction than people who do not. Building more parks would therefore make people happier.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choices: Homes near parks are much more expensive, so the people who live there tend to have higher incomes.
Parks require regular maintenance.
Many parks have playgrounds.
Some people never visit parks.
Life satisfaction can be measured in several ways.
explanation: If residents near parks are wealthier, higher income may explain their satisfaction, not the parks.

passage: In the city's election, every candidate who spent more than one million dollars won. Candidate Rao won.
stem: Which of the following can be properly concluded?
choices: None of the other choices can be concluded from the statements.
Rao spent more than one million dollars.
Rao spent less than one million dollars.
Every winner spent more than one million dollars.
No candidate who spent less than one million dollars won.
explanation: Big spenders all won, but winners need not be big spenders. Rao's win tells us nothing about Rao's spending. This is the classic error of reversing a conditional.

passage: The researchers claim that a gene variant makes people more likely to enjoy bitter foods, because people with the variant reported liking bitter foods more often.
stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim?
choices: In a taste test where participants did not know what they were tasting, those with the variant rated bitter samples more highly.
The variant is common in some countries.
Bitter foods include coffee and dark chocolate.
Some people without the variant also like bitter foods.
The study surveyed over a thousand people.
explanation: A blind taste test removes the influence of food culture and self-image on reports, directly linking the variant to how bitterness tastes.

passage: Our survey of gym members found that 90 percent exercise at least three times a week. So most adults in our country exercise regularly.
stem: The argument's main flaw is that it
choices: draws a conclusion about all adults from a sample unlikely to represent them
uses a percentage instead of a number
does not define exercise
assumes that gym members exercise only at the gym
fails to say when the survey was taken
explanation: Gym members are far more likely to exercise than adults in general, so the sample is biased.

passage: A city lowered the speed limit on a main road from 50 to 30 kilometers per hour. In the following year, accidents on that road fell by half. The city credits the lower limit.
stem: Which of the following would be most helpful in evaluating the city's claim?
choices: How accident numbers changed that year on similar roads where the limit was not lowered
How many drivers received speeding tickets
Whether the road was repaved recently
How many people live along the road
Whether drivers liked the new limit
explanation: Comparing with similar roads shows whether accidents fell everywhere, for some other reason, or only where the limit changed. Repaving could matter too, but a comparison group tests the claim more directly.

passage: A new medicine reduces the risk of heart attack in trials. Yet in the year after it went on sale, the number of heart attacks recorded in hospitals rose.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps resolve the apparent discrepancy?
choices: A more sensitive test introduced the same year detected many mild heart attacks that previously went unrecorded.
The medicine is expensive.
Some patients stopped taking the medicine.
The medicine was tested on adults only.
Heart attacks are more common in winter.
explanation: If detection improved, recorded numbers can rise even while true risk falls. Patients stopping the medicine would not explain an increase above earlier levels.

passage: Since online courses cost less to run than classroom courses, the university can save money by moving its introductory courses online.
stem: Which of the following is an assumption the argument requires?
choices: Moving the courses online will not create new costs large enough to cancel the savings.
Students learn better online.
Most students prefer online courses.
Classroom courses will be discontinued entirely.
Online courses are a recent idea.
explanation: Savings depend on the switch not adding costs, such as new software or support staff, that outweigh the lower running costs.

passage: Because the town's new recycling program has collected twice as much material as the old one, it must be reducing the amount of waste sent to the landfill.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
choices: Much of the material collected under the new program is contaminated and is sent to the landfill anyway.
The new program collects every week instead of every two weeks.
Residents were given new recycling bins.
Recycling programs are common in nearby towns.
The landfill is near the edge of town.
explanation: If collected material ends up in the landfill anyway, collecting more does not reduce landfill waste.

passage: Most employees at the firm work from home on Fridays. Everyone who works from home on Fridays has a laptop issued by the firm.
stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Most employees at the firm have a laptop issued by the firm.
Everyone with a firm laptop works from home on Fridays.
No one works at the office on Fridays.
Some employees without laptops work from home.
Most laptops are used only on Fridays.
explanation: Most employees work from home on Fridays, and all of those have firm laptops, so at least most employees have one.

passage: Ecologists argue that wolves reintroduced to the park reduced the deer population, allowing young trees along rivers to recover.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologists' argument?
choices: Tree recovery was greatest in areas where wolves hunted most often, and weakest where they rarely went.
Wolves also eat smaller animals such as rabbits.
The park has had several wet years since the reintroduction.
Tourists come to the park to see wolves.
Deer numbers in neighboring regions were stable.
explanation: A match between where wolves hunted and where trees recovered supports the causal chain. Wet years would suggest an alternative cause.

passage: Professor Lin's theory about language learning must be wrong. After all, she has changed her mind about several other theories in the past.
stem: The reasoning is flawed because it
choices: attacks the person who holds a view rather than the evidence for the view
relies on too few examples
assumes that theories never change
confuses language learning with other subjects
uses an unclear definition of theory
explanation: Changing one's mind in the past says nothing about whether this theory is correct. The argument targets the person, not the evidence.
